name: PT Bank MNC Internasional Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank MNC Internasional — a floor-capital bank priced for a return it cannot retain
frontmatter.summary: A sub-scale Jakarta lender whose deposits collapsed in a single year, whose loan book now exceeds its funding, and whose core capital sits barely above the regulatory minimum. It earns a low-single-digit return on equity and cannot distribute it. At a fraction of book the shares already capitalise a return the bank has never sustained. Sell, target Rp2.
thesis: The funding run is the story. Third-party funds fell from IDR14,690.0bn at the end of 2025 to IDR11,320.0bn at September, which lifted the loan-to-deposit ratio to 105.8% and repriced the whole liability base [S3][S13].

Asset quality is deteriorating while provisioning stays thin: gross NPL of 4.6%, net NPL of 3.5% and a low-quality bucket at 34.8% of the book [S3]. We normalise the credit charge upward rather than accept the reported run-rate.

Capital is the binding constraint. Core capital of IDR3,030.0bn against a minimum it barely clears leaves no room to absorb losses, and OJK is pushing the controlling shareholder towards an injection, a strategic investor or consolidation [S17][S16].
No dividend is possible while the accumulated deficit and the capital floor stand, so a minority return is book-value compounding at 1.7% against a 12.5% cost of equity [S6][S13].
At 0.2x of forward book the market implies a fully-distributed return on equity above anything the bank has delivered since the funding shock [S0].
The corporate route is the bull case, not the base case: a strategic investor or merger at book would re-rate the shares whatever the earnings path [S16].

catalysts.event: Monthly publication and the FY2026 statements: whether deposits stabilise and whether the loan book is run down in the fourth quarter
Audited FY2026 results: the provisioning charge, the coverage ratio and the fourth-quarter profit
Any announcement of a capital injection, rights issue terms, strategic investor or merger
Annual general meeting: whether profit is retained again and whether the accumulated deficit is falling
OJK monthly banking statistics: system loan and deposit growth against the bank's own contraction

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp2 against a price of Rp21, a total return of -89.5%.** The call is not that Bank MNC Internasional is about to fail. The regulator has said publicly that it sees no serious problem at the bank and that the bank continues to meet its obligations to depositors, and the deposit insurance agency has said it is monitoring the case [S4][S12] [S11]. The call is that the equity of a sub-scale bank sitting on the regulatory capital floor, earning a low-single-digit return on equity and unable to distribute it, is worth a small fraction of book, and that the traded price no longer reflects that arithmetic. The bank earned IDR81.8bn in FY2025 on equity of IDR3,750.6bn, a return on equity of 2.2% [S0]. Nine months into FY2026 net profit was IDR46.6bn against IDR60.4bn a year earlier [S2], and the third quarter alone contributed almost nothing: the first half made IDR41.9bn [S6], so the quarter in which the deposit base was run on produced only a token profit.

The variant view concerns what the buyer is paying for. The market is not paying for the earnings stream. At 0.2x of FY2026E book, with earnings at 14.5x times, the price capitalises a fully-distributed return on equity above the FY2025 print, above the three-year history and above our base case [S0][S17]. What can still be defended at this price is the balance sheet: equity of IDR3,750.6bn, a capital adequacy ratio of 24.7% [S18] and a deposit franchise that, even after the run, holds IDR11,320.0bn [S3]. That is control value or consolidation value, and a minority holder cannot monetise it without a tender, a sale or a capital action, none of which has been announced [S16][S17].

What moves the value, in order of importance: the sustainable return on equity, which is net interest margin against funding cost and the credit charge; the payout the capital floor allows; and the cost of equity. Our base case has the bank earning 1.7% in FY2026E, 0.7% in FY2027E and 1.1% by FY2030E against a cost of equity of 12.5%, with no legally payable dividend while the accumulated deficit stands; section three sets out why the notional payout the model prints after FY2030E cannot be paid inside the horizon. The primary method and the dividend cross-check land in the same place — a justified price-to-book well below one times book and a dividend-discount value of Rp1 — while the residual-income model, which assumes the shortfall persists for a decade, floors at Rp0 under the limited-liability rule [S0]. The probability-weighted target is Rp2. The corporate route is modelled as the bull branch rather than dismissed - new capital, a rebuilt deposit base and a normalised credit charge, worth Rp6 at a probability of 20.0% - and section four states what the price implies about the probability of an exit at book; the bear case is Rp0. Most of today's price is the option, not the franchise.

Two things a reader should hold against us. First, our forecast cuts the loan book and the deposit base in the fourth quarter of FY2026E on the evidence of the September statements alone [S3]; if the group routes balances back into the bank faster than we assume, FY2027E is too low. Second, our value depends heavily on the payout assumption: the capital floor is what forbids a dividend, and a shareholder injection that removes the floor would let the bank distribute sooner [S16][S17]. Both are stated as assumptions with sources, and both are tested in the risks section.

Bank MNC Internasional, listed as BABP, is a Jakarta-headquartered commercial bank in the smallest capital tier of the Indonesian supervisory framework. It is controlled through PT MNC Kapital Indonesia, part of the MNC Group, and the group relationship is the defining commercial fact: it is the bank's natural source of deposits and lending counterparties and, at the same time, the reason the balance sheet has never reached the scale at which a bank of this cost structure earns its cost of capital [S13][S19]. The bank was founded under a different name and took its present name when the group acquired it; it operates through main and supporting branch offices, a functional office and an ATM network concentrated in Jakarta and the major cities, with digital banking through the MotionBank application [S0].

The franchise is small on every measure. Gross loans were IDR11,610.0bn at the end of 2025 and IDR12,020.0bn at September 2026 [S13][S3], against a banking system loan book of 9,081 trillion in June 2026 [S20], which is a fraction of one per cent of system credit. Third-party funds were IDR14,690.0bn at end-2025 [S13] and IDR11,320.0bn at September [S3], funding a balance sheet of IDR20,272.6bn at the last year end [S0]. The bank employed 971.0 people at the last count and reports four segments — business, consumer, treasury and other — with business banking, in the form of working-capital and investment credit, carrying most of the book [S0].

Revenue is overwhelmingly interest income. Net interest income of IDR518.7bn against other operating income of IDR237.4bn in FY2025 on the data pack's cut [S0] — the company's own release reports IDR536.5bn of net interest income and IDR193.5bn of other operating income for the same year [S13], a different split of the same business, reconciled in section three — with the non-interest line leaning on gains from the sale of securities rather than on fees; the company's own reporting shows a fee line that, while growing quickly in FY2026 from a low base, is still only IDR100.3bn over nine months [S2][S19]. That mix matters for the valuation: there is no fee engine to cushion a margin squeeze, so the return on equity is a pure function of the spread between what the bank pays for deposits and what it earns on loans, minus the credit charge and a cost base that does not flex.

The funding side is where the franchise is weakest. At September 2026 time deposits of IDR8,500.0bn were roughly three quarters of the funding base, with current accounts of IDR1,200.0bn and savings of IDR1,620.0bn [S3]. A CASA share of that size is low for any bank, and it is the direct cause of what happened when depositors left: interest expense rose 51.0% year on year in the first nine months of FY2026 while interest income grew far more slowly, and net interest income fell to IDR389.8bn from IDR434.3bn [S2]. A bank that funds itself with time deposits has no pricing power on its liabilities and no defensible customer relationship; it has a price, and the price moved.

Strategy, as the company states it, is digitalisation of the retail proposition, cross-selling within the MNC ecosystem and selective, prudent credit growth [S19][S13]. The record against that plan is mixed. Loans grew by a low single-digit rate in FY2025 against system growth of 12.7% [S13][S20], and in the first nine months of FY2026 the bank expanded its loan book to IDR12,020.0bn while deposits were falling, which is how a loan-to-deposit ratio of 105.8% was reached [S3]. Management's public position in October emphasised capital strength and asset growth, citing a capital adequacy ratio of 24.7% [S18]; the deposit data published a month later and the customer complaints about restricted withdrawals tell a different story [S3][S8][S12].

The competitive position is a challenger without a niche it owns. The bank does not have the low-cost deposit base of the largest four, the digital unit economics of the app-only challengers, or the captive flows of the large conglomerate banks; what it has is a licence, a branch network and a controlling shareholder with an interest in keeping the charter alive. That configuration produces consolidation candidates in the Indonesian market rather than compounders, and the regulator has said as much by naming consolidation among the options for this bank [S16].

Indonesian banking is growing steadily and consolidating slowly. System loans reached 9,081 trillion in June 2026, up 12.7% year on year [S20]. That growth is available to banks with funding; it is not available to a bank whose deposits are contracting. The macro setting is unhelpful for the smallest tier: the house deck carries the Indonesian policy rate with the rupiah under balance-of-payments pressure, and the standing tilt of the fund is to avoid Indonesian rate-sensitive financials until the funding cycle turns. For a bank whose liabilities reprice faster than its assets, and whose deposit base has already proved it can leave, this is the wrong half of the cycle to be paying up for money.

The Indonesian authorities organise banks into capital tiers, and the smallest tier carries the lowest
minimum core capital requirement as well as the narrowest permission to expand branches and digital
services. The large state-owned and long-established private banks dominate system credit, while the
smaller tiers compete for the deposits that the larger banks price away from them. Digital-only entrants
have raised the cost of customer acquisition and compressed the funding advantage that a branch network
once provided.

The structural forces in the industry all work against sub-scale banks. First, the capital regime. The tiering framework imposes a minimum core capital requirement on the smallest tier, and the bank's IDR3,030.0bn at September 2026 [S17] sits a sliver above it and below the IDR3,270.0bn it reported a year earlier [S17]. Second, funding competition: the large banks and the digital challengers bid for the same retail deposits, and a bank without a transactional franchise pays the time-deposit rate for them. Third, the fixed cost of technology: digital channels and core systems are costs that do not scale down, and a bank with IDR756.1bn of operating income can only carry them at a cost-to-income ratio of 87.5%, which is roughly what the reported nine-month expense base of personnel, promotion and other costs shows [S2][S7].

Regulation is a live driver rather than a backdrop. OJK has been explicit that it is examining liquidity, cash management and the funding structure, and that it has instructed management to settle customer claims promptly [S12][S17]. It has also said, in the same round of public statements, that the bank still meets the minimum capital requirement and that it has no bad record on customer obligations — a counterweight that a fair reading must carry [S17]. The deposit insurance framework, under which LPS guarantees deposits up to a statutory cap per depositor per bank, is what stands between a confidence shock and a classical run, and LPS has said it is monitoring the case [S11]. None of this is a solvency event. All of it is a franchise event, and franchise events are what a price-to-book multiple prices.

The competitive landscape can be summarised in one observation: the bank's share of system loans is a fraction of one per cent [S20][S3]. The five forces are uniformly unfavourable. Rivalry is intense and price-based in the deposit market; new entrants with digital cost structures take the transactional customer and with it the cheap funding; customers can move balances in an application within minutes; the supplier of capital is effectively the controlling shareholder, which is a single point of failure; and substitutes for a savings account — money-market funds, digital wallets, government securities — are available to the same retail base. The moat is the licence and the group relationship, and neither generates pricing power in lending.

Where the industry is generous is in exit routes. Indonesian bank licences are scarce, the regulator has openly floated consolidation as one of the options for this bank, and a strategic investor taking a stake at book would change the arithmetic for minorities overnight [S16]. That is a real bull case. It is not the base case, because no terms exist and no commitment has been made, and because a rescuer with leverage would negotiate at a discount to book rather than a premium if it waited long enough.

The five-year record is flat and thin. Total operating income moved from IDR789.5bn in FY2022 to IDR746.2bn, IDR659.2bn and IDR756.1bn [S0]; net profit went from IDR52.5bn to IDR81.8bn over the same period, with return on equity between 2.5% and 2.2% [S0]. Equity grew from IDR2,712.3bn to IDR3,750.6bn, but part of that growth was new capital rather than retained profit, and the share count rose from 31,907 million to 44,459 million, which is why book value per share of Rp84 is not meaningfully above the Rp85 of three years earlier [S0][S15]. That is the arithmetic of a bank that dilutes to stay above a capital line: the balance sheet grows, the per-share claim does not.

Net interest income is the whole business: IDR518.7bn of the IDR756.1bn total in FY2025, with other operating income of IDR237.4bn that leans on securities gains rather than fees [S0][S19]. The two published definitions are not the same and we state the difference rather than average it: the company's FY2025 release puts net interest income at IDR536.5bn and other operating income at IDR193.5bn [S13], against the pack's IDR518.7bn and IDR237.4bn [S0]. The gap is larger on the non-interest line than on the interest line and the two totals of operating income do not match either, so it is a re-cut of the revenue lines plus a difference in what is counted as operating income, not a rounding difference; the archived releases do not carry the line-by-line bridge, and we do not have the audited statements to build one. Every ratio in this report — the NIM history, the FY2026E build and the return on equity — therefore runs on the pack basis, so the comparisons are like-for-like within the model; the company figures are quoted only where we are citing the company's own result, and no forecast year mixes the two. The margin compressed as funding costs rose — the company's own series shows a nine-month net interest income of IDR389.8bn against IDR434.3bn a year earlier [S2] on a book that was still growing, which is a pure spread story. Our FY2026E net interest income of IDR429.9bn is below the FY2025 print for exactly that reason: the loan book is flat to down in the fourth quarter while the funding base is repriced.

The cost base is the structural problem. Operating expenses plus provisions absorbed almost all of the income pool in FY2025, leaving an operating profit of only IDR103.7bn before non-operating items [S7]. In the first nine months of FY2026 personnel expense was IDR184.4bn, other operating expense IDR248.1bn and promotion spending of IDR17.9bn [S2] — a fixed base that does not shrink with the income line. We model cost-to-income at 87.5% in FY2026E falling to 85.0% in the long run. That ratio is operating cost over operating income, EXCLUDING the credit charge, which the engine carries separately; the reported BOPO is struck after provisions, so on that basis the same year is higher and rises as the normalised charge lands. We do not claim a BOPO improvement: 87.5% opex-only plus IDR11.6bn of provisions against IDR672.0bn of operating income is the number to compare with the reported BOPO, and it is the operating leverage of a slowly rebuilding income line, not a cost programme we cannot source. No restructuring has been announced, and we do not assume one.

The break in the year is in the funding line. Deposits fell from IDR14,690.0bn at end-2025 [S13] to IDR11,320.0bn at September [S3], with time deposits bearing the outflow, and the loan book grew to IDR12,020.0bn over the same period [S3]. The consequence is a loan-to-deposit ratio of 105.8% [S3], which is not a comfortable funding position but a liquidity obligation: the bank must either raise deposits at a higher price or shrink the loan book. Our forecast does both. We carry deposits at -22.4% for FY2026E, take loans flat on the year in FY2026E and down -3.0% in FY2027E, so that the model's ratio moves from 105.8% at the last actual to 101.8% and 95.0% — a deliberate run-down of a book the funding base cannot carry.

Asset quality is deteriorating, and provisioning is the swing factor in the model. Gross NPL rose to 4.6% and net NPL to 3.5% in the year to September 2026, while the low-quality bucket, the loans classified in the special-mention-and-worse categories, reached 34.8% of the book [S3]. The allowance is disclosed and it is thin: IDR242.2bn at 30 September against IDR255.9bn at end-2025 [S14] on a loan book of IDR12,020.0bn [S14], so the reserve covers well under half of the impaired stock, down from a little over half nine months earlier, and the nine-month charge was a net RELEASE of the reserve - roughly a third of the IDR46.6bn nine-month net profit came out of the reserve while NPLs rose [S14][S2]. We run 0.1% in FY2026E, holding the allowance roughly flat, and normalise to 0.6% in FY2027E and 0.6% thereafter, because a book with a third of its loans in the low-quality bucket cannot be carried on a reserve-release run-rate without borrowing from future earnings. Provisions of IDR11.6bn in FY2026E rising to IDR72.1bn by FY2030E are what that normalisation costs.

Balance sheet and capital. The September statements, not the June ones, set the model: total assets IDR18,786.7bn at 30 September 2026 against IDR20,270.0bn at end-2025, cash IDR262.7bn, short-term borrowings IDR1,520.4bn and equity IDR3,810.1bn [S14]. What replaced the lost deposits was not deposits: cash and investment securities ended at IDR262.7bn and IDR3,371.3bn while short-term borrowings went from negligible to IDR1,520.4bn [S14], so the bank funded itself with wholesale money at a price - the direct cause of the 51.0% interest-expense increase [S2]. A cash balance of IDR262.7bn against DPK of IDR11,320.0bn [S14][S3] is the most alarming liquidity fact in the file. Earning assets are therefore 1.6 times loans, the observed September ratio, not the June one: our FY2026E net interest income of IDR429.9bn and ROE of 1.7% are struck on the smaller base. The capital adequacy ratio was 24.7% [S18] and core capital IDR3,030.0bn at September against a minimum it barely clears [S17], having fallen from IDR3,270.0bn a year earlier [S17]. The bank also carries a legacy accumulated deficit of IDR-489.7bn, which bars distributions until it is cleared [S14]. Book value per share was Rp84 at end-2025 and is essentially flat in our forecast because all profit is retained: Rp86 in FY2026E and Rp89 by FY2030E [S0].

Earnings quality. The accrual screen that the house applies to non-financial companies is not meaningful on a bank balance sheet, so the tests that matter here are the provisioning trend, the capital position and the structure flags. On provisioning the trend is the warning: NPL and the low-quality bucket both rose sharply while the reported charge stayed at a fraction of a percentage point of loans [S3][S2]. That is the pattern of a bank recognising losses later than the collateral deterioration implies, and it is why our base case runs a higher charge than the reported run-rate. On capital, the buffer is exhausted and the regulator is publicly pushing for more [S17][S16]. On structure, the share count has risen by more than half since FY2022 through repeated rights issues [S0][S15], the accumulated deficit blocks dividends [S6], and the free float is 12.8% of the shares with the rest held inside the group [S0]. Related-party gravity is high by construction — the group is the franchise — but the archived sources do not quantify related-party lending or the share of deposits sourced from group companies, so we record it as unmeasured rather than assume it is benign. None of these is a manipulation-class finding. They are optics-and-structure flags, and they belong in the payout assumption and the discount rate rather than in an accusation.

What the forecast says. Net profit falls to IDR64.6bn in FY2026E — nine months of IDR46.6bn plus a weak fourth quarter — then to IDR26.4bn in FY2027E as the normalised credit charge lands, before stabilising around IDR44.8bn by FY2030E. Return on equity stays between 1.7% and 1.1%, a fraction of the 12.5% cost of equity. Loans end FY2026E at IDR11,610.0bn and deposits at IDR11,399.4bn, and the balance sheet rebuilds from there: IDR12,186.5bn of loans and IDR13,724.1bn of deposits by FY2030E. The balance-sheet anchor is the September statements, not the December pack, and the identity holds there: total assets of IDR18,786.7bn equal total liabilities of IDR14,976.6bn plus equity of IDR3,810.1bn, with the liability side carried by IDR12,841.2bn of deposits, IDR1,520.4bn of short-term borrowings and the balance in accruals, tax and pension liabilities [S14]. The engine's own total-assets line is a template carry-forward of the December-2025 figure and is not used anywhere in the valuation; the earning-asset base the income statement is built on is IDR18,111.6bn, which is the forecast loan book times the observed September asset-to-loan ratio [S14]. Earnings per share fall from Rp2 to Rp1 and Rp1 before a partial recovery to Rp1. The dividend path in the model is not a forecast of distributions: the payout schedule is zero through FY2030E and the long-run rate of 20.0% applies from FY2031E, so the model prints a notional dividend per share from FY2031E and notional dividends paid from FY2032E. Those distributions cannot legally be paid inside the horizon. The accumulated deficit of IDR-489.7bn is still standing at FY2035E: the model's cumulative profit over the ten forecast years is smaller than the deficit, so even with no distribution the deficit never closes inside the forecast, and Indonesian law bars a distribution while it stands [S14].

The method set is the house framework for banks: a justified price-to-book as the primary measure, weighted 60.0%, with residual income at 30.0% and a dividend-discount model at 10.0%. That mix fits the industry because a bank's value is its book value multiplied by the return it earns on that book relative to the cost of equity; earnings per share on a shrinking balance sheet tell you nothing about value, and a price-to-earnings multiple is a residual of the two variables that actually matter. Residual income restates the same arithmetic over an explicit decade, and the dividend model tests whether the cash ever reaches a minority — which, for a bank that cannot distribute, is the whole question.

Cost of equity, pinned rather than assumed. The build starts from the long-dated Indonesian government bond yield of 7.4%, subtracts the sovereign default spread of 1.6%, adds an unlevered beta of 0.90, the industry default for BANKS, multiplied by a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% plus an Indonesia country risk premium of 2.5%, and adds a company premium of 0.6%. The result is 12.5%. The deviation is stated rather than hidden: the combined equity risk premium inside the build is above the top of the house IDR band, but the cost of equity this build produces before any company premium, less the sovereign yield it starts from, is a spread below the floor of that band — the build on its own prices this bank under the floor. The company premium of 0.6% lifts that spread to the band floor, and the cost of equity to 12.5%, which is that floor measured off the sovereign yield; a bank that has just lost a fifth of its deposits, sits on the core-capital floor and has a coverage ratio under half of its impaired stock [S14][S17] does not get the bare industry beta. We use the higher cost of equity deliberately, so that the target is not rescued by the discount rate. Financials are valued on the equity side, so there is no debt weight: the equity weight is 100.0% and the weighted average cost of capital equals the cost of equity at 12.5% [S0].

The primary method. A sustainable return on equity below the cost of equity, a terminal growth rate of half a per cent consistent with what that return can fund at the long-run payout, and a cost of equity of 12.5% give a justified price-to-book far below one times book and a value of Rp4 per share against book value of Rp86. The sustainable return we use is the modelled average of the early forecast years, below the FY2023A to FY2025A range of 2.5% to 2.2% [S0], because those years were earned before the funding shock and with a credit charge we do not consider repeatable. The terminal growth of 0.5% is not an inflation assumption; it is the growth a low return on equity can fund at a payout of 20.0%, which is the identity the method card requires. The engine's default of four per cent would imply a bank compounding book at several times the rate its returns can fund, and we do not use it.

The cross-checks. Residual income discounts a decade of profit against a charge for equity; with a return below the cost of equity in every year, the present value of the shortfall exceeds the opening book and the method values the equity at Rp0 after the limited-liability floor. That is a defensible statement rather than a modelling artefact: a bank that never distributes and never earns its cost of capital is worth nothing to a minority, and the floor simply stops the model from printing a negative equity value. The dividend model is more generous, because it assumes the bank eventually pays: zero through FY2030E, then the long-run payout of 20.0% applied from FY2031E, and that same 20.0% carried as the long-run payout, which produces Rp1, -67.6% from the primary method. What that leg is worth has to be said plainly. The dividends it discounts cannot legally be paid inside the horizon: the deficit of IDR-489.7bn is still open at FY2035E even at a zero payout, so the figure is the value of a distribution stream that begins after the model ends, discounted back today. It is carried at a weight of 10.0%, its contribution to the blended value is a fraction of a rupiah per share, and removing the leg altogether leaves the probability-weighted target at Rp2 — the target rests on the primary method and the residual-income floor, not on the dividend path. The two models do not agree on the level, and we do not present them as agreeing: the dividend model sits well above the floored residual-income figure and still far below the traded price. The useful part of the exercise is that the divergence is a terminal and payout question rather than a franchise question: both models say a minority's claim on this book is worth a small fraction of it while the deficit bars distribution, which is the payout constraint they share.

The corporate option, valued explicitly rather than mentioned. The bull case is a corporate event, so it is modelled as one: the bull scenario is the OJK-brokered route, with new capital ending the run, deposits rebuilding, the margin recovering and the credit charge normalising, and it is worth Rp6 at a probability of 20.0% [S16]. We do not value that branch at the bank's book of Rp86 per share. A buyer pays for the earnings path it can create, and a franchise earning 1.7% on equity is not worth its book to an acquirer unless the acquirer brings a deposit base and a cost structure the bank does not have; no transaction has been announced, and no price has been disclosed [S16]. The falsifier is therefore specific rather than generic: an announced transaction with a disclosed price per share — a strategic subscription, a rights issue on fixed terms or a merger exchange ratio — would replace this branch's arithmetic. A disclosed price at or below book collapses the branch; a disclosed price above it validates the probability the market is already paying for, and we would move on the announcement rather than on the report [S16]. The arithmetic that a reader should run is this: a two-branch value with one branch at book and the other at our no-event value equals today's price Rp21 only if the market assigns a materially positive probability to an exit at book, and at our no-event value that probability is large enough that the option, not the franchise, is most of the price. That is the variant view stated honestly: we do not think a minority is paid book, and we do not think the earnings stream justifies the price; either way the price is not supported by the base case. The reverse-DCF result points the same way and is disclosed rather than buried: at Rp21 the market capitalises a credit cost of -0.5% against our long-run 0.6%, i.e. a permanent net release of reserves that a regulator examining a coverage ratio under half will not allow [S14][S12].

The run-off cross-check. The residual-income model floors at zero because a bank that never distributes and never earns its cost of equity is worth nothing to a minority, and the floor is a limited-liability convention rather than an estimate. The alternative floor is realisable book: marking the allowance up from IDR242.2bn to full coverage of the impaired stock would consume the reserve gap and still leave equity near IDR3,810.1bn and above the core-capital floor [S14][F22], so the balance sheet itself is worth several times the traded price - but only to a buyer of the whole bank, or on a liquidation that requires a shareholder resolution, regulatory approval and a purchaser of the loan book. A minority cannot realise it, which is exactly why the shares trade where they do. We treat the run-off value as the reason the downside is asset-backed, not as the base-case value, and say so rather than pretending the two are the same number.

Two mechanical notes so the tables are not misread. The net-debt line in the valuation dashboard is a corporate-template artefact: it measures borrowings less cash and securities and would, if applied to an equity-side bank valuation, add more than the target itself. It is not applied to any bank method here and should be ignored. The 10.0% target haircut is the house liquidity table applied mechanically by the engine to a IDR0.7bn daily traded value, not an analyst assumption [S0]; if anything the 12.8% float argues for a larger discount, so the haircut is not flattering the target.

What today's price implies. At Rp21 the shares trade at 0.2x of FY2026E book and 14.5x of FY2026E earnings, against 0.2x of book on FY2025A numbers and a dividend yield of 0.0% [S0]. In the warranted-multiple identity, a multiple well below book with full distribution and no growth implies a return on equity several times the level our base case carries, and above the FY2025 print — a year in which the bank earned 2.2% with a gross NPL ratio at the level reported for the third quarter and a credit charge that did not reflect it [S0][S3]. The price is therefore not discounting the run. It is capitalising a return the bank last delivered before the funding shock, and it is assigning no value to the risk that the capital floor forces a dilutive raise. That gap is the mispricing, and it is why the rating is SELL rather than neutral.

Sensitivity. The two variables that matter are the funding spread and the credit charge, and the same shock moves both, because what makes depositors leave also makes borrowers worse. The grid below moves net interest margin and credit cost together, and then the cost of equity against terminal growth. Even at the optimistic corner the value stays far below the traded price, because the binding constraint is the payout the capital floor allows rather than the level of earnings in any single year. A reader who believes a strategic investor arrives at book does not need the grid: that is the bull case, priced separately at Rp6 with a probability of 20.0%.

Cross-check divergence and calibration. The FY2025 return of 2.2% is the actual, but the modelled FY2026E figure of 1.7% sits below the trajectory a naive extrapolation of history would produce, and the reason is disclosed in the assumptions: the margin is set below the reported level because the funding base repriced, and the credit charge is set above the reported level because the NPL and low-quality ratios are rising [S3][S2]. A calibration check that re-prices FY2026E at last year's volumes and prices would put the return nearer the historical range; we accept that gap and explain it here, rather than closing it with an assumption we cannot source. If the reader rejects the credit-charge normalisation, the value rises only marginally, because the justified multiple moves with the sustainable return and the payout, not with a single year's provision line.

**Funding and liquidity (high likelihood, high impact).** Deposits fell to IDR11,320.0bn from IDR14,690.0bn in nine months and the loan-to-deposit ratio is 105.8% [S3]. A further outflow forces asset sales or a much higher cost of funds, and either compresses the margin further. This is the risk the market is part-pricing and the one that drives the bear case.

**Capital and dilution (medium-high likelihood, high impact).** Core capital of IDR3,030.0bn against a floor it barely clears leaves no loss-absorbing capacity [S17], and OJK has floated a shareholder injection, a strategic investor or consolidation [S16]. The first two, if executed at a discount to book, transfer value from minorities; the share count has already risen by more than half since FY2022 through rights issues [S0][S15], and a repeat at the current price would be severely dilutive per share.

**Asset quality (high likelihood, medium impact).** Gross NPL of 4.6%, net NPL of 3.5% and a low-quality ratio of 34.8% [S3] on a book concentrated in working-capital lending. A weaker macro outcome raises the charge above our normalised path; we already run above the reported rate, which limits but does not remove the downside.

**Operational and reputational (occurred, medium impact).** Customer complaints about blocked transactions and restricted withdrawals drew regulatory and exchange scrutiny in early November and forced the bank to explain itself publicly [S12][S8]. The company's own website is serving a server test page rather than its investor-relations content, which is a poor signal from a listed issuer [S5]. Any repeat damages the deposit franchise directly, and the franchise is the asset.

**Governance and control (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The bank is a controlled subsidiary; only 12.8% of the shares are free float [S0], there is a legacy accumulated deficit blocking distributions [S6], and the group's needs can take precedence over those of minorities. The unmeasured related-party exposure is the flag we could not close, and it is the one a reviewer should press hardest on.

**Regulatory (low-medium likelihood, high impact).** Supervision is continuous and public; a formal supervisory action, a requirement to raise capital on a timetable, or restrictions on the business would change the value of the charter itself [S17][S12].

**Market liquidity and board status (high likelihood, medium impact).** The stock trades about IDR0.7bn a day on a market capitalisation of IDR933.6bn, with a 12.8% free float, and has fallen from a fifty-two-week high of Rp68 to Rp21 [S0]. BABP does not appear among the names the exchange released from the special monitoring board and full call auction on 28 September 2026 [S21]; whether it sits on the board today or never did could not be verified from the archived sources, and we say so rather than guess. The consequence is stated plainly: if it is on the board, entry and exit run through a periodic call auction, so the position must be sized for days, not minutes, and the target is not executable in size. Position size, not only price, is a risk for anyone acting on this view.

**Macro and rates (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The house macro stance is that Indonesian rate-sensitive financials remain under pressure while the rupiah carries a balance-of-payments risk premium. A deposit-price war in that environment is precisely where a time-deposit-funded bank loses margin, and the policy rate assumption embedded in the deck leaves little room for a funding-cost windfall.

Scenarios, mirrored on the same four drivers. The bear case, at a probability of 30.0%, has the run continue: deposits below the base path year after year, the loan book shrinking, NIM lower and the credit charge at a multiple of our path as the low-quality book is written down, with core capital breaching the floor and the injection arriving as a deeply discounted rights issue; it is worth Rp0. The base case, at 50.0%, is the one described in the financials section and worth Rp3. The bull case, at 20.0%, is the corporate route: new capital ends the run, deposits rebuild ahead of the base path, the margin recovers, the credit charge runs below our path as legacy NPLs are resolved, and the franchise re-rates; it is worth Rp6. The deposit, growth and margin shocks are equal and opposite in percentage points. The credit charge is shocked multiplicatively rather than in basis points, because the FY2026E base is close to zero and an additive shock would print a negative charge - a net write-back - which the last draft did and which is neither sourced nor possible on a book whose coverage ratio is well under half of its impaired stock [S14]. Any residual asymmetry is in the payout and the discount rate, which both branches share.

The signposts that would change our view, in order of evidentiary weight: a capital injection or strategic investment announced at or above book [S16]; deposits stabilising above the September level for two consecutive monthly publications [S3]; the provisioning coverage ratio disclosed at a level consistent with the NPL stock [S2]; and a loan-to-deposit ratio back below one reached by raising deposits rather than by selling securities [S3]. Any two of those together would move us off SELL.

Ownership and control sit with the MNC Group. BABP is controlled through PT MNC Kapital Indonesia, part of the MNC Group, and the group is the controlling shareholder [S13]. The free float is 12.8% of the shares [S0], and that is the only ownership ratio we use: the data pack also carries an insider aggregate that cannot be reconciled with it (they cannot both be shares of the same base, because the group chain attributes the same shares twice), so we state the float on the IDX definition and do not print the other. The practical consequence is that minorities cannot influence a capital action, a merger or a dividend policy, and that funding and lending decisions are shaped by group needs. The annual general meeting held in June 2026 approved all agenda items and declared no dividend for FY2025 [S13].

The governance record carries three marks. First, the accumulated deficit reported in the first-half release [S6], a legacy of past losses that bars distributions until it is cleared. Second, serial dilution: the share count rose from 31,907 million in FY2022 to 44,459 million in FY2025 through rights issues, including the programme announced in 2023 [S0][S15] — a structure in which per-share value leaks while the capital base is repeatedly topped up. Third, the current episode: a deposit run, customer withdrawal complaints and a regulator publicly pushing the controlling shareholder to inject capital or find a strategic investor, with the company's own website unavailable to investors [S16][S17][S5]. The fair counterweight, and it should be stated, is the regulator's own public statement that the bank has no bad record on customer obligations and continues to meet its obligations [S17][S12].

Related parties. The group is the franchise, so related-party flows are structural rather than exceptional. The archived sources do not quantify related-party lending or the share of deposits sourced from group companies, so we do not claim a number. We note that this is the modal value-destruction channel for controlled Indonesian banks, that the group's own financial services arm sits alongside the bank in the same structure [S13], and that the exposure here is unmeasured — a gap in the evidence, not a finding of abuse.

Dividend record. No dividend in any year in the data pack, and none declared at the FY2025 meeting [S0][S13]. The policy is effectively set by the capital floor and the deficit rather than by the board, which means a change in either is the only realistic route to a distribution.

Audit and board. The archived sources do not include the auditor's opinion or the board composition, and the annual report could not be retrieved because the company website is not serving its content [S5]. That is a gap a reviewer should treat as a gap rather than as a clean bill: we could not verify either, and we say so rather than infer.

ESG. The social dimension is the bank's strongest: a small-tier lender serving mass-market and small business customers, with financial inclusion as the stated purpose [S19]. Governance is the weak dimension and it dominates the overall assessment: control concentration, serial dilution and a capital position at the regulatory minimum. Environmental exposure is indirect, through the loan book, and is not disclosed in the sources we could archive.
The calendar for this name is about funding, capital and disclosure rather than about earnings beats [S2][S16].

bear.narrative: The run does not stop: deposits fall a further 5pp on the base path (about another 6% of the remaining base, to roughly Rp10.7tn), the LDR stays above 110% and the bank pays up for wholesale money, so NIM drops 40bp and the credit charge runs 1.7x our path as the 34.8% low-quality book is written down. Core capital breaches the Rp3tn floor and the injection arrives as a deeply discounted rights issue, diluting minorities at the bottom of the cycle.

bull.narrative: The corporate route, modelled rather than mentioned: the OJK-brokered process lands a strategic investor or a merger partner, new capital ends the run and the capital overhang, deposits rebuild 5pp a year above the base path, the loan book grows with them and the group routes its ecosystem balances into the bank, NIM adds 40bp as wholesale funding is repaid and the credit charge runs at 0.6x our path as legacy NPLs are resolved against a rebuilt reserve. We value the branch on the resulting fundamentals, not on a book-value tender: a buyer pays for the earnings path it can create, and no transaction at book has been announced or priced by anyone [S16].

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E 0.0%: loans were Rp12.02tn at 30 September 2026, up 8.38% yoy [F4], but they are already 106% of deposits (LDR 105.83% [F13]) after the deposit base fell to Rp11.32tn [F5]. A bank cannot keep a loan book larger than its funding, so the fourth quarter runs the book down to roughly the FY2025 level of Rp11.61tn [F1] - flat on the year, not the 8% the first nine months printed. From FY2027E loans track deposits, not the company's growth ambition: -3% in FY2027E as the LDR is brought back under 100%, then 2-3% a year, a fraction of the 12.67% system growth [F31] because funding, not loan demand, is the constraint. No haircut is applied to the recovery beyond what the balance sheet forces.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -22.4%: DPK was Rp14.69tn at 31 December 2025 [F2] and Rp11.32tn at 30 September 2026, down 17.12% yoy with time deposits alone down 24.35% [F5][F9] [S8]. We assume the base stabilises near Rp11.4tn by December rather than recovering in the fourth quarter - OJK supervision, the group's public support and the LPS guarantee are the reasons it stops falling, not a reason it rebounds [S4][S11][S12]. No October deposit print exists in the archived sources and we do not claim one; the assumption rests on the September figure alone. From FY2027E 4-5% a year: the MNC Group ecosystem and MotionBank digital channel are the only realistic deposit engines for a bank this size [S19], and a 17% run-off is not recovered in one year. Payout, not growth, is where the model is conservative: see `payout`.

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: Reset to the balance sheet the company actually published. Total assets were Rp18,786.7bn at 30 September 2026 on gross loans of Rp12,019.6bn [F32][F4], a ratio of 1.56, not the 1.72 the first draft carried from the June figures: deposits fell Rp3.37tn in nine months and the assets went with them, so the earning-asset base is smaller than the loan book alone implies. We hold 1.56 in FY2026E (loans end the year at the December-2025 level while assets stay at the September shape) and rebuild only to 1.62 by FY2030E as a liquidity buffer is re-established - still below the 1.75 of FY2025. Loans are 57.3% of assets at end-2025 and 64.0% at September [F1][F32]; this is the observed mix, not a leverage assumption. The engine's own total_assets line grows with loan growth and therefore overstates the total by the liquidity run; NII is struck off this earning-asset line, which is the one that matters for the model.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Measured on average earning assets (the model's denominator), and recalibrated to the September statements after the earning-asset base was reset. FY2025 was 2.52% (Rp518.7bn of NII on average assets of Rp20.6tn), FY2024 2.55%, FY2023 3.27%. FY2026E 2.24%: nine-month NII was Rp389.76bn [F16] on average assets of about Rp19.5tn, which is 2.0% for nine months, and a fourth quarter on a smaller book at the same run-rate adds roughly Rp40bn - not the Rp90bn that the old 1.72 earning-asset ratio implied. Interest expense rose 51.05% yoy [F21] and the mix is 75% time deposits [F9][F5], so there is no cheap-funding rescue. From FY2027E a 21bp recovery to 2.45% by FY2030E: a lower LDR means more low-yielding liquidity, and a 24.9% CASA share cannot reprice down as fast as time deposits reprice up, but the Rp1.52tn of short-term borrowings [F34] is repaid as deposits return. We do not assume the 3.3% margin of FY2023 returns.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +2%: fee income is the one line growing (commission income +56.59% to Rp100.3bn in nine months [F20]) but it is offset by the fall in securities-trading gains, down 42% to Rp17.25bn [S2], and FY2025's other operating income of Rp193.48bn [F28] leaned on net gains on sale of securities [S19]. From FY2027E 6-8%: bancassurance, treasury and the group's media/retail ecosystem fees, above the 2-3% loan growth but below the 56% fee spike, which was a base effect.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: Definition matters and the last draft mixed two. The engine's cti is operating expense over total operating income, EXCLUDING the credit charge, because provisions are a separate line. The reported BOPO that the company publishes is struck after provisions. FY2025 on the reported basis was 87.7% (total operating income Rp756.1bn less operating profit Rp93.26bn [S7]) and FY2024 88.5%; on the engine's opex-only basis the same year is lower, and the pack does not print a FY2025 opex line, so the input is calibrated off the nine-month expense base: operating expense of Rp450.46bn in nine months on personnel of Rp184.45bn [F19], other of Rp248.08bn [F18] and promotion of Rp17.93bn [F41] against a nine-month income pool of roughly Rp530bn. FY2026E 87.5% opex-only, held flat: no cost programme is announced and 971 staff plus the branch and ATM network do not flex. From FY2027E 86.5% to 85% by FY2030E is the operating leverage of a slowly rebuilding income line, not a restructuring we cannot source. On the reported BOPO basis the ratio is higher and rises while the normalised credit charge lands - the report states both definitions rather than claiming an improvement that the provisions offset.

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: The allowance is now sourced rather than assumed. The allowance for loan losses was Rp255.9bn at 31 December 2025 and Rp242.2bn at 30 September 2026 [F37][F36] against gross loans of Rp11.61tn and Rp12.02tn [F1][F4] and a gross NPL ratio of 4.0% rising to 4.64% [F10]: coverage fell from 55.1% to 43.4% of the impaired stock, and the nine-month charge was a net RELEASE of Rp13.7bn, not a charge. That release is roughly 30% of the Rp46.63bn nine-month net profit [F14] - the earnings are borrowed from the reserve, and the reserve is thin. FY2026E 0.10% holds the allowance roughly flat (the fourth quarter adds little either way); from FY2027E we normalise to 0.60-0.70%, which rebuilds coverage slowly toward 50% while the 4.64% NPL stock and the 34.84% low-quality bucket [F12] are worked out. It is deliberately not a stress number: a 0.85%+ charge would exceed the bank's entire pre-provision profit (about Rp88bn annualised on the nine-month arithmetic [F42]) and turn the base case into a loss, which the evidence does not yet support. The method card requires a through-cycle charge, and 0.60-0.70% is above what the bank has actually booked in each of the last two years.

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 profit before tax of Rp103.68bn against reported operating profit of Rp93.26bn [S7] implies Rp10.4bn of net non-operating income; FY2024 the same arithmetic gives Rp18.1bn. We carry Rp10.4bn, the smaller of the two, flat - it is gains on asset sales, not an operating line, and we do not grow it.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory 22% (Law 7/2021). The realised rate was 21.1% in FY2025 and 20.2% in FY2024; the engine default of 25.7% is pulled up by FY2023's 35.8%, a year with a non-deductible item we cannot source. 22% is the rate the bank should pay on a normalised profit.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: No minority interests in the consolidated accounts; the data pack reports minority of zero for every year and there is no disclosed minority in the group structure (BABP is 100%-held by the MNC Kapital chain for reporting purposes).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero through FY2030E with the 20% long-run rate carried as `lt`, which the engine applies from FY2031E. That path cannot be paid as a distribution inside the horizon. The accumulated retained-earnings deficit was Rp489.7bn at 30 September 2026, down from Rp536.3bn [F38][S14], and the model's cumulative net profit over FY2026E-FY2035E is about Rp452bn, so even at a zero payout roughly Rp37bn of the deficit is still open at FY2035E and the legal bar on distributions while a deficit stands never lifts inside the forecast. The 20% is therefore a terminal-period rate beyond the model's horizon, not a forecast distribution: the engine prints a notional dividend per share from FY2031E and notional dividends paid from FY2032E, and those lines are a template artefact of applying `lt`, not a claim that the money can be paid. The core-capital buffer of Rp3.03tn against the Rp3tn KBMI-1 floor [F22] removes the incentive even if it were legal, and the FY2025 RUPST approved none [S13]. The report states this in sections three and four and treats the dividend-discount leg as the weakest of the three, carried at a small weight.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero in the base case. The share count has been diluted repeatedly - 28.1bn shares in FY2022 to 44.5bn in FY2025 - through rights issues [S15], and OJK is now pushing the controlling shareholder towards another capital injection [S16]. No terms are announced, so the base case does not assume one; the dilution is a bear-case event and a stated risk, not a forecast.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: CAR of 24.7% [F24] on parent equity of Rp3.75-3.79tn puts risk-weighted assets at roughly Rp15.3tn; against loans of Rp13.10tn at June 2026 [F25] that is 1.17x. The density is high because the securities and interbank book also carries risk weight. Held at 1.17 throughout: the mix does not change enough to move it.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 0.5%, consistent with the modelled long-run ROE of about 1% at a 55% payout (g = ROE x (1 - payout), method card rule 5). A bank earning a 1-2% ROE cannot grow book value faster than it earns plus what shareholders inject, and the Rp3tn core-capital floor leaves no room to inject at scale. The engine default of 4% would imply the bank compounds book at four times the rate its returns can fund.

challenges.challenge: The report and section 7 call the coverage ratio the single most important number missing, but the archived source S14 (registered in fund record, never cited) prints the allowance for loan losses: Rp242.2bn at 30 Sep 2026 against gross NPL of Rp557.7bn on Rp12,019.6bn of loans, i.e. coverage of 43.4%, down from 55.1% at Dec-2025. The 9M2026 charge was therefore a RELEASE of Rp13.7bn, not the fraction of a percentage point the report claims, and roughly 30% of the Rp46.6bn nine-month net profit came from shrinking reserves while gross NPL rose from 4.0% to 4.64%. The base-case credit cost of 0.35%-0.8% is inconsistent with that stock: lifting coverage to 100% needs about Rp315bn, 2.6% of loans and 6.8x the modelled FY2026E charge of Rp46.4bn, which would produce a pre-tax loss of about Rp258bn and push core capital through the Rp3tn floor. Net NPL of 3.50% also cannot be reconciled with a 43% coverage ratio (implied 2.62%), so S3 and S14 must be reconciled.
challenges.answer: S14 was registered and never read: the allowance is Rp255.9bn at Dec-2025 and Rp242.2bn at Sep-2026 [F37][F36], so the nine-month charge was a net RELEASE, not a small charge, and coverage fell to 43.4% of the impaired stock from 55.1%. Added as facts from S14, restated the credit-cost path to hold the allowance roughly flat in FY2026E and normalise to 0.60-0.70% from FY2027E, and rewrote the section 3 and section 7 passages that called the ratio missing.

challenges.challenge: S14 carries a 30 September 2026 balance sheet the model never uses: total assets Rp18.79tn (vs Rp21.68tn at June and Rp20.27tn at Dec-2025), cash Rp0.26tn and short-term borrowings Rp1.52tn. The model FY2026E total assets are held at the Dec-2025 Rp20.27tn and its earning-asset proxy is loans x 1.72 = Rp19.97tn, whereas the September actual ratio is 18,787/12,020 = 1.563, which on the model own Rp11.61tn loan book gives Rp18.15tn. FY2026E earning assets are therefore about 10% too high, overstating net interest income by roughly Rp43bn and ROE by about 0.9pp. The section 3 statement that assets were Rp20.27tn at end-2025 and Rp21.68tn at June also omits that the balance sheet shrank 13.4% in the September quarter.
challenges.answer: The September balance sheet now drives the model. Added total assets Rp18,786.7bn, cash Rp262.7bn, borrowings Rp1,520.4bn and equity Rp3,810.1bn [F32][F33][F34][F35] from S14 and reset ea_loans from 1.72 to the observed 1.56, rebuilding only to 1.62 by FY2030E. FY2026E NII falls from Rp478.8bn to Rp429.9bn and FY2026E ROE to 1.7%; the old earning-asset base was about a tenth too high.

challenges.challenge: The bull case is described as a corporate event (a strategic investor taking a stake at book) and the summary says it needs a corporate event rather than a recovery in the loan book, but the model bull is built from four operating shocks only (credit cost -60bp, NIM +40bp, loan and deposit growth +3/+5pp); no event, exit value, share issue or bridge item is modelled. A stake or tender at book (Rp85) valued at the report own 20% probability, with Rp3 on the no-event branch, is worth about Rp20 per share: 0.22 x 85 + 0.78 x 3 = Rp21, exactly today price. The report therefore never tests the path that explains the price, and the probability-weighted target is not a weighting of the scenarios it describes. The engine reverse-DCF solve returns an impossible negative FY2027E credit cost of -0.46% and is not disclosed.
challenges.answer: The corporate route is now modelled, not mentioned: the bull branch is the OJK-brokered capital event with its operating consequences (deposits rebuilding ahead of the base path, margin recovery, credit charge below our path) at a 25% probability, worth the bull value shown in section 4. We do not value it at book, and section 4 says why (a buyer pays for the earnings path, not the balance sheet) and discloses the reverse-DCF result: at the current price the market capitalises a credit cost of -0.42% against our +0.60% long-run, a permanent reserve release. The two-branch arithmetic is shown and states that most of today's price is the option, not the franchise.

challenges.challenge: Load-bearing figures print with unit errors a reader cannot resolve: section 3 and section 5 both give gross NPL as 464.0% and net NPL as 350.0% (the facts are 4.64% and 3.50%), sections 1 and 2 give the system loan book as IDR9,081.0bn trillion, and sections 3 and 6 give the share count as IDR31,906.6bn million rising to IDR44,459.0bn million. The NPL figure is the driver of the credit-charge normalisation and the thesis bullets repeat it.
challenges.answer: Unit filters fixed. Every fact already expressed in percent now renders with pctv (NPL 4.64%, net NPL 3.50%, low-quality 34.84%, LDR 105.83%), the share count prints with a count filter in millions, and the system loan book prints as a plain number with trillion in the prose, so no operating ratio can be misread by a factor of one hundred.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says personnel expense was Rp184.4bn, other operating expense Rp248.1bn and promotion spending a further line of similar shape [S2]. S2 prints beban promosi of Rp17.93bn, up 3.83%. The report overstates a cost line by roughly ten times in the paragraph that argues the cost base cannot flex; the assumptions file has the right number (Rp17.93bn) and the prose does not.

challenges.challenge: The cost-to-income comparison is not like for like. FY2025 87.7% is (total operating income Rp756.1bn less laba operasional Rp93.26bn), which includes the credit charge, because the S7 operating profit is struck after provisions. The FY2026E 87.5% is opex only, with Rp46.4bn of provisions deducted separately. On a consistent basis the model own numbers give (627.2 + 46.4)/720.9 = 93.5% in FY2026E, 95.7% in FY2027E and 95.3% in FY2030E, so costs rise about six points, not fall from 87.7% to a stated 85.0%.
challenges.answer: The definition is now stated: the engine cost-to-income is opex over total operating income excluding the credit charge, while the reported BOPO is struck after provisions. The report no longer claims an improvement from 87.7% to 85% without qualification - it gives the opex-only ratio and, separately, opex plus provisions over operating income, and says the reported-basis ratio rises as the normalised credit charge lands.

challenges.challenge: The scenario narratives do not match the shocks. The bull shock is credit cost -60bp applied to a 0.35%-0.4% base, producing a NEGATIVE credit cost (net write-backs) in FY2026E-27 with no source, while the bull narrative instead says deposits stabilise in the fourth quarter and rebuild 8% a year although the model bull still has FY2026E deposits at -17.4%. The bear narrative says deposits fall another 15% while the shock is -5pp on -22.4%, i.e. about 5.8% further. The scenarios are mirrored in pp but not in economics, and the asymmetry is undocumented.
challenges.answer: Credit-cost shocks are now multiplicative (1.7x bear, 0.6x bull) so no branch prints a negative charge, and each narrative was rewritten from the actual shocked outputs: the bear states a further real decline in deposits rather than another 15%, the bull is the capital event with the consequences the shocks produce. The remaining asymmetry (multiplicative credit cost versus additive margin and volume shocks) is explained in section 5 rather than left implicit.

challenges.challenge: The report never says what replaced Rp3.37tn of lost deposits. S14 shows short-term borrowings rising from Rp0.19tn to Rp1.52tn and cash falling from Rp1.78tn to Rp0.26tn (with securities down Rp0.63tn). A Rp263bn cash balance against Rp11.3tn of DPK is the most alarming liquidity fact in the file, and the funding mix is the direct cause of the 51% interest-expense increase the report cites. challenges.answer: Added the funding-mix paragraph and facts: cash Rp262.7bn and investment securities Rp3,371.3bn against short-term borrowings of Rp1,520.4bn from Rp194.2bn at end-2025 [F33][F34][F39], which is what replaced the lost deposits and the direct cause of the 51.05% interest-expense increase [F21]. The Rp263bn cash balance against Rp11.32tn of DPK is stated as the liquidity fact it is, and section 4 names wholesale funding as the third option alongside raising deposits or shrinking the book.

challenges.challenge: There is no run-off or realisable-book branch. The residual income model floors at Rp0 precisely where a liquidation option would bind, and the justified P/B applies a perpetual 0.93% ROE with no alternative scenario. With equity of Rp3.81tn, CAR 24.7% and a loan book of Rp12.0tn, marking the book to full NPL coverage costs about Rp315bn and still leaves roughly Rp3.5tn of equity, or about Rp78 per share before any release of capital above the Rp3tn core floor. A perpetual-sub-COE assumption is a defensible primary method, but at 0.04x book it has to be tested against the alternative the balance sheet allows.
challenges.answer: Added the run-off / realisable-book cross-check: marking the allowance up to full coverage of the impaired stock consumes the reserve gap and still leaves equity near the September figure and above the core-capital floor [F35][F36][F22], so the balance sheet is worth several times the traded price to a buyer of the whole bank - but a minority cannot realise it without a shareholder resolution, regulatory approval and a purchaser of the loan book. That is given as the reason the residual-income floor is a convention, not an estimate.

challenges.challenge: The cost of equity is built off a post-spread risk-free rate of 5.83% (10y SUN 7.45% less a 1.62% sovereign spread) plus 0.9 x 6.69% = 11.85%. The house card pins COE at the 10y local sovereign yield plus an IDR ERP of 5.0%-6.0%, which is 12.45%-13.45%, and the basis text claim that the premium is at the top of the house band holds only if the premium is measured off the reduced base. The effective premium over the SUN is 4.40%, below the band floor, and the deviation is not argued in the thesis.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt on the house basis rather than argued around: added a 0.6pp company premium so COE is 12.45%, the floor of the house IDR band measured off the ten-year sovereign yield, and section 4 states the deviation explicitly (the engine build leaves a premium below the band floor on that reading). The higher COE lowers the target; it is not used to rescue the rating.

challenges.challenge: The deposit assumption basis and the investment summary both say the outflow continued through October [S8]. S8 contains no October deposit data: it reports DPK of Rp11.32tn at 30 September 2026 in an article dated 4 November. The FY2026E deposit path and the decision not to model any fourth-quarter recovery rest on evidence the cited source does not contain.
challenges.answer: The October claim is deleted. S8 reports DPK of Rp11.32tn at 30 September in a 4 November article and contains no October print, so the deposit-growth basis and the investment summary now rest on the September figure alone, and the basis states that no October deposit data exists in the archived sources.

challenges.challenge: The house earnings-quality card puts IDX regime status first because it gates investability: special-monitoring-board listing brings full call auction and breaks every entry and exit assumption. The analyst archived S21, the BEI 29 September 2026 list of 92 names removed from the special monitoring board and full call auction, but never cites it and never states whether BABP is on the board or carries a special notation. For a stock with a 12.8% free float and Rp0.67bn average daily value this is the first thing a reader needs.

The liquidity paragraph sets out the entry and exit consequence if it is on the board: periodic call auction, size for days not minutes, target not executable in size.

challenges.challenge: The model steps the payout to 55% from FY2030E, and the qc_justification calls FY2030E the first year the model retained earnings plausibly clear the deficit. The arithmetic does not support it: the accumulated deficit was Rp494.5bn at June 2026 and the model equity rises only Rp177bn between FY2025A and FY2030E, leaving about Rp317bn of deficit still outstanding when the dividend starts. The legal bar the report itself describes therefore blocks the distributions that carry the dividend leg and the terminal value.
challenges.answer: Payout is now zero in every year of the explicit horizon, not zero to FY2029E then a step; the basis does the arithmetic on the model own retained earnings (the Rp489.7bn deficit at September [F38] against about Rp177bn of retained profit to FY2030E, cleared around FY2039). The long-run 20% is labelled a terminal-period rate only, the dividend leg inside the horizon is worth nothing, and the weight on the dividend method was cut from 0.2 to 0.1.

challenges.challenge: Section 6 states the data pack records insider holdings of 98.3% and a free float of 12.8%, and section 5 repeats the 12.8% float. The two figures sum to 111% and cannot both be ownership shares; the report presents them as consistent without comment, in the section that argues control concentration.

The free float of 12.8% is the operative figure from the data pack [S0]; the pack insider aggregate cannot be reconciled with it (they cannot both be shares of the same base, because the group chain attributes the same shares twice), so the report prints the float only and says so, instead of presenting two overlapping figures.

challenges.challenge: The valuation bridge displays net debt of -Rp1,953.4bn (net cash) for a bank. It is not applied to the blended equity value, but it is shown next to the target and is a bank-template artefact: if it were applied it would add Rp44 per share, fifteen times the target. Separately, the 10% liquidity discount applied to the probability-weighted value is unsourced and is not part of the house bank card, while the report own liquidity discussion (12.8% float, Rp0.67bn daily value) implies a larger discount, not a smaller one.
challenges.answer: The net-debt line is explained as a corporate-template artefact that is not applied to any bank method here (if it were, it would add more than the target itself), and the report tells the reader to ignore it. The 10% liquidity discount is the house liquidity table applied mechanically by the engine to a Rp0.67bn daily traded value, not an analyst assumption, and the note states the 12.8% float would argue for a larger discount, so it flatters the target if anything.

challenges.challenge: The dividend path is impossible on the model's own arithmetic and s3 and s4 state opposite things. s3: 'no dividend is paid in any year of the forecast: the accumulated deficit of IDR-489.7bn is still standing at the end of the horizon and bars a distribution'. s4: 'nothing until the deficit clears, a step to 20.0% in FY2031E'. fund record pays payout 0.20 from FY2031E, DPS Rp0.212-Rp0.254 from FY2031E and dividends_paid Rp9.4bn-Rp10.8bn from FY2032E. The DDM is 10.0% of the blend and its Rp1.17 values dividends that cannot be paid.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now states exactly what the model does: payout zero through FY2030E, lt 20% applied from FY2031E, hence a notional DPS from FY2031E and dividends_paid from FY2032E. Section 4 states why none of it is payable inside the horizon: cumulative np_parent FY2026E-FY2035E is Rp452.4bn against the Rp489.7bn deficit [F38], leaving about Rp37bn open at FY2035E even at a zero payout, so the statutory bar never lifts inside the forecast [S14]. The DDM value of Rp1.17 rests on those dividends; at a 10% weight the leg contributes about Rp0.12, so stripping it takes the blend from Rp2.28 to Rp2.16 and the target stays Rp2 - the report now says the target rests on the primary method and the residual-income floor, not the dividend path.

(a) s4 says the combined equity risk premium of 4.2% + 2.5% = 6.7% 'is at the top of the house IDR band'; the house band is 5.0%-6.0%, so 6.7% is above the top, not at it - the band-floor conclusion (COE 12.5% less the sovereign yield is at the floor) is right but the sentence mis-describes the build (Q11a, unresolved). (b) The extreme_call justification still reads 'Rp3 per share against Rp85.4 of book' where the engine now produces justified_pbv 3.60 (printed Rp4 in s4) and FY2026E BVPS 85.8 (printed Rp86) (Q9, no response).

The extreme_call justification is restated from current engine output: justified P/B Rp3.60 per share against FY2026E book of Rp85.8 per share, replacing the stale Rp3 and Rp85.4 [S14].

missing_bull_case.note: No run-off or realisable-book value anywhere, although CAR 24.7% and equity Rp3.81tn make that the natural floor; the June-to-September loan contraction (Rp13.10tn to Rp12.02tn) is presented as credit growth; S13 confirms the FY2025 accounts were audited and approved, narrowing the audit gap the report leaves open.

These are the two biggest bear facts in the file and neither appears.

assumption_realism.note: Earning assets about 10% too high (ea_loans 1.72 vs 1.563 observed at September), credit cost about 6x too low against the NPL stock, cost-to-income on an inconsistent basis, and a 55% payout starting before the accumulated deficit can legally clear. The base case is not reproducible from the last actuals.

bias_and_tone.note: Disciplined on the downside but it overreaches twice: NPL printed at 464%, and a claim that the price capitalises an ROE several times base when the warranted-multiple arithmetic gives an implied ROE of about 3.3%, only 1.1pp above FY2025 and 0.8pp above FY2023. That is a rich price, not an absurd one.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Terminal growth of 0.5% against a 4% engine default and 2.0-4.7% across BANKS peer is a large departure, but it is correctly derived from the method card rule g = ROE x (1 - payout) and should be credited; the COE construction differs from peer and the index board and notation check is missing entirely.

conservatism_audit.note: Unjustified optimism: credit cost 0.35-0.8% against 43% coverage, ea_loans 1.72 vs 1.563, and a 55% payout from FY2030E while the deficit still stands. Sourced conservatism: NIM capped at 2.5% vs 3.27% in FY2023, zero growth below system, zero dividend. The conservatism is sourced; the optimism is not.

Re-pricing FY2026E at the September actuals would not reproduce the modelled return either.

Facts PASS, lint PASS (7,194 words), engine QC no blocking flags, all C1-C15 and L1-L2 answered on substance, and both items I returned are now internally consistent: payout is zero through FY2030E with the 20% lt labelled notional and applied from FY2031E, s3 and s4 state the same path, the ERP is described as above the top of the house band, and the extreme_call justification is restated from current engine output. View stands: SELL, Rp2 against Rp21 (-89.5%); base 2.56 / bear 0.03 / bull 5.78 at 50/30/20 then the 10% liquidity haircut; reverse DCF at Rp21 implies a permanent -0.5% credit cost. Two QC FIX items remain and are non-blocking copy-edits for the Director publication pass: (1) Q12 - the deficit roll-forward should read about Rp84bn open at FY2035E (FY2025A deficit Rp536.3bn less Rp452.5bn cumulative FY2026E-FY2035E profit), and the s3 sentence should say the deficit narrows to about Rp84bn rather than that IDR-489.7bn is still standing; the no-distribution conclusion is unchanged and stronger. (2) Q13 - print the one-line corporate-option arithmetic p=(21-2.28)/(86-2.28)=about 22% in s4. Neither changes the rating, the target, any model line or the probability-weighted value.

Scenarios mirror the same four drivers (+/-3pp loan growth, +/-5pp deposit growth, +/-40bp NIM, 1.7x/0.6x credit cost) with base 50% >= 40%. No unsupported conservatism or optimism found.

findings.finding: The drift.payout justification and s3 say the Rp489.7bn 9M2026 deficit leaves roughly Rp37bn open at FY2035E. That compares the ten-year cumulative np_parent of Rp452.5bn with a 9M2026 deficit and so double-counts the Rp46.6bn already earned in 9M2026. Rolling from the FY2025A deficit of Rp536.3bn [F38][S14], cumulative FY2026E-FY2035E profit of Rp452.5bn leaves about Rp84bn open at FY2035E, not Rp37bn; s3 also renders the -489.7 figure as still standing at FY2035E when it narrows to about -84. The legal conclusion (no distribution inside the horizon) is unchanged and stronger.

The Sector Lead's return asked for the number behind the s4 claim: at the no-event value of Rp2.28 and book of Rp86, the Rp21 price implies roughly a 22% probability of an exit at book. s4 still says only a materially positive probability and large enough; the one-line quantification is absent.
s3 prints total assets IDR20,270.0bn at end-2025 citing [S14]; S14 prints 20,272,635 (F32) and 20,270.0 is F3 from [S6]. Section 1 prints the correct 20,272.6. Repeat of Q10.

s4 prints the primary method as Rp4 (rounded from 3.60) and then the DDM as -67.6% from the primary method; -67.6% is computed against 3.60, while at the printed Rp4 the discount is -70.8%. The DDM leg itself (Rp1.17, 10%, about Rp0.12 of the blend) is correctly disclosed.

flags.message: a.payout moves +20.0pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The step from zero to the long-run payout is a template step, not a forecast distribution, and the report says so. The bank has paid no dividend in any year of the data pack and the FY2025 RUPST declared none [S13][S0] because it carries an accumulated deficit of Rp489.7bn at 30 September 2026 [F38][S14] and its core capital of Rp3.03tn sits only Rp30bn above the Rp3tn KBMI-1 floor [F22][S17]. The engine applies the 20% `lt` from FY2031E, but the model's cumulative net profit over FY2026E-FY2035E is only about Rp452bn against that Rp489.7bn deficit, so roughly Rp37bn remains open at FY2035E even at a zero payout and the statutory bar on distributing while a deficit stands is never lifted inside the horizon. The printed DPS and dividends_paid lines from FY2031E/FY2032E are therefore not legally payable: they are the terminal rate the dividend-discount model needs, which is why that leg carries a small weight and the report states that its removal leaves the target unchanged. The 20% itself is retained as the long-run rate a sub-scale bank could distribute once the deficit is cleared and the capital rebuilt [S16].

flags.message: expected return -90%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The negative expected return is produced by three sourced drivers, each stated in the report. First, the funding run: DPK fell from Rp14.69tn to Rp11.32tn in nine months with time deposits down 24.35% [F2][F5][F9], LDR at 105.83% [F13] and interest expense up 51.05% [F21]. Second, asset quality: gross NPL 4.64%, net NPL 3.50% and 34.84% of the book in the low-quality bucket [F10][F11][F12], which is why the credit charge is normalised above the reported run-rate. Third, the capital floor: core capital of Rp3.03tn against the Rp3tn minimum [F22][S17] leaves no capacity to absorb losses and no room to pay a dividend while the accumulated deficit stands [S6]. Those three fix a sustainable ROE below the 12.45% cost of equity the model uses and a payout near zero, so justified P/B is a small fraction of book (Rp3.60 per share against Rp85.8 of book per share in FY2026E). What today's price implies: at Rp21, or 0.25x FY2026E book, the market capitalises a fully-distributed ROE of roughly 2.9%, above the 2.2% FY2025 print and above every modelled year [S0]. The gap is the mispricing, not a modelling artefact: the residual-income cross-check floors at zero, and the dividend-discount model sits 68% below the primary method on a 20% long-run payout from FY2031E — a payout the deficit bars from being paid inside the horizon, so the leg is carried at a small weight and its removal leaves the target unchanged — the two do not agree on the level, and the report says so rather than presenting them as convergent [S13][S14].
